title: Ethiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops enter Tigray
description: Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BB
body: Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BBC Eritrean troops had crossed into the country.In a letter sent to the UN Security Council and seen by the BBC, Ethiopia's foreign minister called it a "blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence".Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel responded by saying it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from its neighbour.Fighting broke out two weeks ago between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended a civil war.Ethiopia says Eritrea is backing the TPLF, which it denies.During the two-year civil war, Eritrea was a key ally of the Ethiopian government, having fought alongside them against the TPLF. But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated - largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports - leading to the severing of diplomatic ties last week.Accusing Eritrea of violating its sovereignty, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60km (37 miles) into Tigray.Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted Eritrean forces in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war.US-based conflict monitor Acled said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in Adigrat were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight.One resident told AFP news agency "there were many, many drone strikes", and that some Eritrean lorries had been destroyed.Another witness said Eritrean forces appeared to be retreating north after the strikes, AFP reported.There have so far been no verified reports of casualties. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray.Dated 8 October, Ethiopia's letter to UN Security Council members read: "In this time of difficulty, when Ethiopia is left with no other option but to defend itself, we count on your understanding, support, and solidarity."But while Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of supporting the TPLF, Eritrea has blamed the conflict on Ethiopia's leaders, and accused them looking for a reason to seize Eritrean territory.On Friday, Eritrea's information minister called the accusations levelled against Asmara as "duplicity in their most extreme forms".In a post on X, he said Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition".Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, but ties were only normalised in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power.This latest unrest follows months of tension and the launch of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia - including the TPLF - in September.Last week, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control.

schema.headline: Ethiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops enter Tigray

title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a 'gift to Putin'
description: President Donald Trump has announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US, as he faces mounting pressure to bring down fuel prices.Trump said P
body: President Donald Trump has announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US, as he faces mounting pressure to bring down fuel prices.Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.The move on Friday sparked anger from Ukraine's President Volodymr Zelensky, who called it a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.In his Truth Social post, Trump added that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period", dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have seen attacks by Ukraine.Putin later said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts.Analysts, however, have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.Tim Armitage, investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot, said the numbers mentioned by Trump were "relatively small". He said the first tranche equated to approximately 2.25m barrels, and daily US consumption was around 3.8m barrels, "so it won't make a material difference to pump prices in the US"."Granted, there are then two more releases to come, but it does appear to be a slightly desperate move by President Trump to try to lower inflation ahead of the midterms."The BBC has asked the White House what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment. Meanwhile, the UK government spokesperson said its position "could not be clearer" and it would continue working with international partners to support Ukraine and bring about sustained peace."We will also maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK, increasing the cost of Putin's aggression and supporting efforts to secure a just and lasting peace."Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US, as he has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which began in February, and its impact on global energy prices.That conflict has sent the cost of petrol and, in particular diesel, skyrocketing in America in recent months, which has soured his standing with the public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation.The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market. Putin said in a statement that he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large."An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."But Zelensky hit out at it, saying "gifts to Putin will not work for peace" and that Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror"."We count on America's fair support for our defence of life, for our defence of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one," he wrote.A spokesperson for the UK government said: "The UK's position could not be clearer. We will continue working closely with international partners to ensure Ukraine has the military and financial support it needs to defend itself." They added that the government would continue to "maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by UK"."Russia could end this war today. We remain committed to supporting Ukraine for as long as it takes and to working with partners to bring about a durable peace."Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.According to the International Energy Agency, its diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%.Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.But Zelensky defended the strikes on Friday, saying there were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector"."Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information and the details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return is unclear. But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US, that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine.What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel.With the looming US midterm congressional elections - which will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain.Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax.Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns, and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

schema.headline: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a 'gift to Putin'

title: Commentator Katie Zacharia picked as new White House press secretary
description: Donald Trump has chosen conservative commentator Katie Zacharia to be the next White House press secretary.Zacharia, who currently works for Trump Med
body: Donald Trump has chosen conservative commentator Katie Zacharia to be the next White House press secretary.Zacharia, who currently works for Trump Media & Technology Group, will become the US president's sixth chief spokesperson across his two administrations. She previously had a brief stint as a spokeswoman at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).Trump called Zacharia "loyal" and "a devoted fan and member of MAGA" in a social media post on Friday, referring to his Make America Great Again movement, adding that she had "an unblemished record of support".Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, who left the White House in August, has reportedly taken a job with Fox News."She was previously involved in my Campaigns, assisting in key Swing States, where we won 7 out of 7," Trump wrote on Truth Social of Zacharia."I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration."Zacharia thanked him in a post on X, writing: "Serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime."She said Trump had "shown America that we can be great again, and he works to effectuate that greatness every single day". She said she looked forward "to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out". The 42-year-old political strategist is a frequent fixture on conservative Newsmax and Fox News, and has been active in Republican politics for most of her adult life, having worked as an intern for the Republican National Committee and for the White House Office of Political Affairs during the Bush administration in 2006.Since June, she has been a senior communications adviser for Trump's media company and Truth Social platform, according to her LinkedIn profile. She worked in Homeland Security from February to March this year.While she was only briefly in government at DHS - which the mother of four later said she left because of the strain of travel between California and Washington on her family - she has long been a ferocious defender of President Trump and his administration's policies.In a June interview with the BBC, for example, she dismissed criticism of Trump's controversial use of the White House to host a televised UFC fight, saying the principles of the UFC "are the kind of principles that founded our Constitutional Republic"."It's about not giving up the fight until the bitter end," she said. "I think there's no better summation of the American ethos than a good UFC fight."Earlier this year, Zacharia wrote an op-ed in the New York Post about an incident in which she was asked to stop wearing a "Make America Great Again" hat to her local gym."I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," she wrote. "This is raw, unfiltered intolerance. Freedom of speech doesn't evaporate at the gym door."Justin Buchler, a political science professor at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio, told the BBC that Trump's appointments during his second term have been "based on personal affiliation and loyalty". "He values loyalty first and foremost," Buchler told the BBC. A lawyer educated at Pepperdine University in California, Zacharia also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally - and current Special Presidential Envoy for Special Missions - Ric Grenell.In 2011, she spent nearly two years clerking at a law firm in Beijing, China.The complex job of press secretary goes beyond the briefing room podium to include managing contentious relationships with the press, coordinating with other parts of the White House, and providing media advice to the president. The secretary also oversees an office that receives a significant amount of inquiries and requests on a daily basis.Yanna Krupnikov, a political scientist and professor of communication and media at the University of Michigan, said the selection of Zacharia "speaks to a blurring of the lines between different media types". Politicians nowadays need to communicate not only to various news outlets but with people in a social media context, she said."I think the goal is not as much speaking to the media and journalists, but making sure that particular, very specific sound-bytes and messages get to ordinary people," Krupnikov told the BBC.When Leavitt left the role, Trump called her one of his "most trusted aides", which sets a high bar for her replacement. Leavitt left because she said she wanted to spend more time with her family.

schema.headline: Commentator Katie Zacharia picked as new White House press secretary

title: Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
description: Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in the US state of Florida and is expected to bring life-threatening flooding and winds that have forced thousands
body: Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in the US state of Florida and is expected to bring life-threatening flooding and winds that have forced thousands to evacuate.The storm weakened slightly to a category 2 hurricane, with 110 mph (175 kph) winds, before ramming into Florida's western panhandle on Friday evening.Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency as meteorologists warned of life-threatening storm surge that could cause up to 9 feet (2.7m) of flooding in some areas. Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El-Niño fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean. Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations due to the storm.  In Florida, those evacuations includes coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Florida Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!"Governor of Alabama Kay Ivey issued a mandatory evacuation for all non-residents, tourists and visitors in key counties likely to be heavily affected by the storm.Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific.It marks the first time in more than 30 years that a hurricane did not form till October.The storm is likely to bring "life-threatening storm surge" to the US Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center warned. After hitting Florida, the centre of Isaias is forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday, the National Weather Service said late on Friday.As of Friday evening, hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles (55 km)  from Isaias' centre, and tropical storm-force winds extended as far as 205 miles (335 km).John Guoth, a resident of Navarre, Florida, told the BBC that he and his wife will remain in their home despite the rest of his street having already left."It's a hurricane, we get them all the time... we kind of knew that when we moved here," he said."Pretty much everything that can fly and will fly is battened down, and everything that cannot fly is really, really secured," he said,Guoth said he put his ducks and chickens in the bathroom and weighed down his boats and trailers so "nothing flips over".A few households have remained in the area, describing them as "long-term locals" who are "going to protect our homes".Pensacola resident Brandin Ruth told the BBC that they have been turning the gas off to the buildings, icing down product and trying to get team members home.People in the Florida city have "seen bad storms before" but are "bunkering up", he said, adding: "You don't want to underestimate a storm like this".Two other storms are also forecast to batter North America this weekend.Hurricane Simon is bearing down on the Pacific coast of Mexico as a category one hurricane. It is set to pick up speed and become category four by Saturday, eventually making landfall near Puerto Vallarta on Sunday, according to Reuters.Further north, Tropical Storm Rachel, a downgraded hurricane, is heading toward landfall around the US-Mexico border, along the Pacific. While, Rachel is expected to reach the coast late on Saturday, the impact of the storm is already being felt due to high tides in southern California.Video footage and photos show several streets under water in Newport Beach, California, through a combination of the tropical storm swells at sea and high tide.Posting on its account on X, the City of Newport Beach advised people to "avoid the Balboa Peninsula due to street flooding caused by recent storm conditions and elevated tides".It also urged people not to drive through flooded streets. Bulldozers have been shoring up the beach to try and prevent further flooding.With additional reporting by Simon King.

schema.headline: Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida

title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
description: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "di
body: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially.However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims.The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel.The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software.Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution.He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution.The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function.Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty".The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred".It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment."This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself.The sanctions could ultimately see the ICC unable to try cases, meaning detainees awaiting trial or judgment could have to be released, according to Professor Ryan Goodman from the New York University School of Law.Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines.The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Others awaiting trial or with pending appeals include former senior figures accused of war crimes in Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic.Goodman says that as a senator, Rubio was "out front" highlighting Duterte's alleged crimes.He told the BBC such a release would be "enormously damaging to the global effort towards international justice [and] towards the Philippines"."[For] the victims, it just has to be incredibly traumatic because a lot of them participate in the ICC proceedings to put themselves on the line with a hope that justice will come around," adds Goodman, a former special counsel at the US Department of Defence.Among the carve-outs announced as part of today's sanctions are "licenses" allowing the ICC to continue "services for the operation of facilities used for the detention" of Duterte and others.However, Goodman says ultimately these detainees may have to be released "as a matter of law" if the financial sanctions mean the court cannot conduct fair trials or appeals.

schema.headline: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'

title: CJP, Gyanesh Kumar: Tens of thousands of forces deployed as Delhi braces for cockroach protest
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Police have been deployed in big numbers even during demonstrations by opposition parties in the lead
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Police have been deployed in big numbers even during demonstrations by opposition parties in the lead up to Saturday's 'cockroach' protest  ByGeeta PandeySocial Affairs Editor, IndiaUpdated 10 minutes agoParts of the Indian capital, Delhi, have been turned into a fortress, with tens of thousands of security forces deployed, as the influential Gen Z-led "cockroach" movement has called for a major protest on Saturday.The protesters are seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists. The Election Commission has denied this and Kumar is yet to comment on the resignation demand.Police say they have denied permission for the gathering and all roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the main protest venue, have been closed with huge metal barricades. The restrictions have caused major disruption across central Delhi, with traffic diverted from several key roads. A journey that would normally take 15 minutes took more than an hour this morning.At Jantar Mantar, metal barricades and ropes have been erected around the protest site, preventing people from entering. Some protesters who arrived early were stopped and questioned by police and paramilitary personnel deployed in the area.At a nearby roundabout, loudspeakers repeatedly broadcast appeals for people to cooperate with the police.In a statement posted on X, Delhi Police defended the measures, saying they were necessary to maintain public safety and prevent overcrowding at Jantar Mantar, which can accommodate only 1,000 people at a time.Image caption, Sabika Muzaffar has travelled from nearby Haryana state with her mother to take part in Saturday's protestSeveral trains to Delhi have also been cancelled and police have ordered dozens of metro stations shut to prevent protesters from gathering.But Abhijeet Dipke, founder ⁠of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) - the online satirical movement that is spearheading the protests - has said the CJP will march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning "come what may"."If you want to jail us or even shoot us we are prepared," he added, addressing ​Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a post on X. The CJP's weeks-long protest in the summer seeking education reforms was its first major challenge to Modi's government. The CJP scored a major victory when it forced education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July.The CJP protesters returned to streets last week with a rally in Mumbai city to press for CEC Kumar's resignation. On Thursday, they held a huge rally in the southern city of Bengaluru (formerly Bangalore).Student groups and opposition parties have also protested in the capital over the past few days.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, The CJP held a rally in Bengaluru city on Thursday against CEC Kumar Saturday's protests are being billed as the biggest in recent times as they are also being supported by several opposition parties, farmer organisations and student groups.CJP leaders allege the authorities have been preventing many of their supporters from reaching Delhi. In the capital, more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed and authorities have appealed to citizens to stay away from protests.Police official Nupur Prasad told a press conference, external that one of the reasons for denying permission to protest at Jantar Mantar was the "short notice" given by the CJP. "Under current guidelines, an application to organise an event at Jantar Mantar must be submitted at least 10 days prior to the scheduled date," she said. Also, she added that in the past, the CJP had not followed "lawful directions" given to them. "In light of the non-compliance with prescribed procedures, the failure to adhere to past legal directions, and the current state of public safety, law and order, and traffic regulation, permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar is hereby denied."The CJP have questioned police denying them permission for the protest - they say that legally they only have to inform the police and do not need their approval to gather.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Gyanesh Kumar is at the centre of the voter-roll revision controversy At the centre of the row is a controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.The Election Commission says it is to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.But opposition parties and activists have alleged that many of those are eligible voters and that the process is being manipulated by CEC Kumar to favour Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.The past few days have also seen a major escalation in the opposition's standoff with the Election Commission.For three days in a row starting Tuesday, Delhi witnessed dramatic scenes with police breaking up protests by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other MPs over the issue.Videos showing police forcing Gandhi on to a bus and preventing him from climbing out of the bus window subsequently went viral on social media.

schema.headline: CJP, Gyanesh Kumar: Tens of thousands of forces deployed as Delhi braces for cockroach protest

title: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design
description: Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the
body: Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo.The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused.The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile.In the Federal Court on Friday, lawyers for White Fox denied any breach of trademark.While White Fox has not yet lodged a formal defence, its lawyers told Justice Ian Jackman that the firm intends to argue that other prominent Australian brands such as Cotton On, Sportscraft and Glassons sell clothes with "similar decorative stripes". Lawyers for Adidas told the court that White Fox, in advertising and selling its clothes with four stripes, had the "intention to trade off our reputation".A three to four-day trial is expected to take place early next year, the court heard.In its written statement of claim, Adidas says its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957.The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark.White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims.It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items.This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim.The company says White Fox is "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind".Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs.Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops.In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes.A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image.In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes.White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024.In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review.

schema.headline: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design

title: Two paintings stolen from Renoir Museum in France are recovered
description: Two paintings by Auguste Renoir stolen a month ago from a museum in the south of France have been recovered, the local town hall has said.The two work
body: Two paintings by Auguste Renoir stolen a month ago from a museum in the south of France have been recovered, the local town hall has said.The two works were seized on 8 September when thieves cut through a fence and smashed a window at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the French impressionist had lived during his final years.The local mayor praised authorities for recovering the paintings and said the news gave immense joy and profound relief.Six suspects have also been arrested in relation with the heist at Renoir Museum, the town hall confirmed in a statement.The theft was the latest in a series of high-profile art heists in Europe.The two missing paintings were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).The thieves had used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings inside the museum and had initially made off with four paintings, but dropped two of them in the museum's garden as they fled"These two paintings are far more than works of art. They are part of our city's history, our cultural heritage and the legacy Auguste Renoir left to Cagnes-sur-Mer," said Mayor Bryan Masson, who is part of France's National Rally.The town hall said initially that it would provide further details of the recovery on Friday, but cancelled a planned press conference.The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks.Opened in 1960, it houses a variety of objects that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters.Earlier this year paintings by Renoir, Paul Cézanne and Henri Matisse were stolen from a museum near the Italian city of Parma, in a raid that lasted just three minutes. They were recovered  in August.France saw its biggest art robbery in years last October, when crown jewels were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris.Disguised as construction workers, the thieves broke into the Louvre's first-floor Apollo Gallery during the museum's opening hours. They used an angle-grinder to open display cases and made off with €88m (£78m) of jewels that once belonged to France's 19th-Century queens and empresses.The Louvre was subsequently criticised for under-investing in security.

schema.headline: Two paintings stolen from Renoir Museum in France are recovered

title: Crazy Rich Asians TV show to reunite Constance Wu and Henry Golding
description: Four of the stars of 2018's Crazy Rich Asians film are reprising their roles for a TV show of the same name. The series will pick up events after the
body: Four of the stars of 2018's Crazy Rich Asians film are reprising their roles for a TV show of the same name. The series will pick up events after the end of the hit film, with Constance Wu and Henry Golding playing their lead roles of Rachel and Nick, while Ronny Chieng is back as Eddie and Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh will have a recurring role as Nick's mother Eleanor. "It's a 'Crazy Rich' family reunion!" said Adele Lim, who co-wrote the film, calling it the sequel we've been waiting for". It will "delve into the characters and worlds of Kevin Kwan's brilliant books" over eight episodes, she said.The show will be made by HBO, and the news was announced days after HBO's parent company Warner Bros announced its £110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Paramount Skydance. Adapted from Kwan's bestseller books, written between 2013 and 2017, the film topped the US box office and was nominated for two Golden Globes.It featured an all-Asian cast and told the story of an Asian-American woman who gets a culture shock meeting her boyfriend's ultra-wealthy family in Singapore.Lim is showrunner for the new TV series and will be one of the executive producers, as will the the film's director Jon M Chu.

schema.headline: Crazy Rich Asians TV show to reunite Constance Wu and Henry Golding

title: Christa Pike's health has seen 'profound turnaround' in last three days, lawyers say
description: Christa Pike has 'profound' health turnaround after botched execution, lawyers sayFigure caption, Watch: What we know about Christa Pike's "shock" rec
body: Christa Pike has 'profound' health turnaround after botched execution, lawyers sayFigure caption, Watch: What we know about Christa Pike's "shock" recovery in hospitalByNardine SaadChrista Pike has made a "profound" turnaround after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, her lawyers say.Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995. She survived two injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September and was taken to hospital in a critical condition.Pike's lawyers described her recovery as "remarkable" and said in a statement on Thursday that she was able to walk with assistance and was eating. She had also regained some movement in her arms, which were badly injured during the attempted execution, they said."Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery," the statement said.The case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.Image source, Reuters"Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die," her legal team said. Pike's lawyers said they do not know the full emotional and psychological toll of the execution attempt or how long it will take her to recover.They added that while she was struggling to process what had happened, she "continues to express concern for others, particularly the family of her victim Colleen Slemmer".Slemmer's mother, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death, has branded the failed execution a "mess".Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty as he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.A court has ordered officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution, which could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.On Wednesday, Judge I'Ashea Myles ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained", including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, such as packaging, inserts and labels.The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition before, during and after the failed execution.She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions for the rest of the year and said he wants answers about what went wrong.Pike's lawyers have called on the governor to downgrade Pike's punishment to life in prison without parole.Proponents of capital punishment have suggested using a different method to put her to death.Killing Death RowCould the US death penalty ever die out? A surreal story about a man in Acton, London, who supplied the USA with lethal drugs tips Livvy Haydock into the macabre world of Death Row.

schema.headline: Christa Pike's health has seen 'profound turnaround' in last three days, lawyers say

title: South African anti-migrant protests: Cars torched and shops looted in Durban and Soweto
description: At least 24 vehicles have been set ablaze and foreign-owned shops looted in South Africa as anti-immigration protests descended into violence in two m
body: At least 24 vehicles have been set ablaze and foreign-owned shops looted in South Africa as anti-immigration protests descended into violence in two major cities, police say. Unrest broke out on Thursday in Soweto, a sprawling township outside Johannesburg, the country's largest city, and Durban, a major port on the east coast.The violence comes amid growing anger over a court ruling which would allow some migrants who had arrived in the country illegally to apply for asylum.This had led to long queues outside immigration centres and the government on Friday said it would change the way it would comply with that ruling, without giving details.The Department of Home Affairs said the current policy had seen its staff "overwhelmed", while "serious threats to public safety and order had emerged".It said that the new policy would still abide by the Constitutional Court ruling.South Africa has experienced repeated outbreaks of xenophobic violence, often targeting migrants from neighbouring countries.Thursday's demonstration turned violent following allegations that a foreign national had assaulted one of the protesters in Durban. Three foreign nationals were arrested in connection with the alleged assault, police said.In Durban, in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal, protesters gathered outside a government refugee reception centre demanding that it stop accepting asylum applications.Police fired rubber bullets to disperse crowds as businesses in the city centre shut their doors."There were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," senior local police officer Xolani Fihla told state broadcaster SABC."At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported," he added.Police said 14 vehicles were torched in Durban and 10 in Soweto, where gunshots were also reported during confrontations between residents and foreign shopkeepers.Acting national police commissioner Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane condemned the destruction of property.In Orlando West, a neighbourhood of Soweto, residents had initially gathered to demand the closure of small convenience stores, known locally as spaza shops, operated by foreign nationals.Protesters forced foreign traders out of some areas, while shops were attacked and a building was set on fire, local media reported. Police said reinforcements had been deployed to prevent further violence.The authorities have promised to pursue those responsible for the destruction.The latest unrest follows a July ruling by Constitutional Court, South Africa's highest court, which struck down restrictions preventing some people from seeking asylum because of how they entered the country or missed immigration deadlines.The judgment means asylum seekers must be allowed to submit applications, even if they entered South Africa without the required documents.This prompted hundreds of people to gather at refugee reception centres, fuelling anger among anti-immigration campaigners who fear the decision will encourage undocumented migration.Government spokesman William Baloyi told Reuters news agency that people had deliberately spread false claims about the judgment, creating the impression that undocumented migrants would automatically be granted legal status.Baloyi insisted that the ruling does not automatically give migrants refugee status or the right to remain permanently in South Africa.Officials say applications will still be assessed individually and applicants will remain subject to immigration checks.Earlier this year, anti-immigration groups staged weeks of demonstrations demanding that undocumented foreign nationals leave the country by 30 June.The protests forced tens of thousands of migrants to flee, with some returning home through repatriation programmes organised by their governments.South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals.The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce.Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence.Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities.Additional reporting by Christian Parkinson in Johannesburg

schema.headline: South African anti-migrant protests: Cars torched and shops looted in Durban and Soweto

title: US immigration officials defend ICE agents who shot man while his child was in the car
description: US immigration officials have defended officers who shot and wounded a man in his car in New York on Thursday while his five-year-old son was in the b
body: US immigration officials have defended officers who shot and wounded a man in his car in New York on Thursday while his five-year-old son was in the back seat.Department of Homeland Security (DHS) chief Markwayne Mullin said officers opened fire while trying to arrest a man with a criminal history."We weren't aware the child was in the car," Mullin said, arguing that it was the man, Oscar Belgal, who had put his child in danger. Belgal is being held at a detention facility. His lawyers appeared at a hearing on his behalf on Friday."The first thing he asked me, is whether his son is OK," his attorney Harold Solis said outside court.A handful of friends and family members, including a cousin and an aunt, attended the hearing but did not speak to the press. Another of his lawyers, Paige Austin, told the judge at the hearing that Belgal "still has a bullet in his body" and had been taken to the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn after being discharged from hospital. Austin said he had only been able to make a brief phone call within the hour prior to the hearing.The BBC has not been able to confirm his medical condition, but contacted DHS and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The shooting happened in the residential neighbourhood of Marble Hill.Marcos Charles, a top ICE official, said the agency's officers used their vehicles to try and stop Belgal in his car but that he resisted orders to get out and instead accelerated, smashing into two ICE vehicles.Charles said Belgal then "weaponised his vehicle and proceeded to accelerate going towards other officers", adding: "Our officers, using their training, and believing that their life and the life of their partners in the general public were in danger, used their training and fired weapons."The number of officers who fired their weapons is being investigated.Charles said Belgal "was struck by one of the bullets or fragments superficially in the neck".New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who called what happened "unconscionable and incredibly serious", said ICE agents surrounded Belgal's car before opening fire."They wore construction vests and masks that concealed their faces. There is no reasonable way to identify them as ICE agents," Mamdani said. He confirmed the child was unharmed.Mullin said the officers identified themselves and were wearing body-worn cameras that were turned on during the incident. Video of the shooting, including body camera footage, has not been made public but unverified videos on social media appear to align with Mamdani's comments. Body-worn camera footage released by the New York Police Department (NYPD) on Friday shows its officers arriving on scene and attempting to help Belgal after he has been shot. One ICE officer appears to be wearing a neon construction vest and carrying a large gun. The NYPD officers then call for an ambulance and put him in a police car to take him to hospital. They are later seen pulling Belgal from the vehicle and carrying him into the hospital.Mamdani said on Thursday that he had spoken to US President Donald Trump and Mullin for two hours but failed to negotiate Belgal's release. Mamdani said he would ask Trump, who has not yet commented publicly on the shooting, to end ICE enforcement actions in New York. Mullin has said he will not pause enforcement. The DHS said Belgal, 28, was from the Dominican Republic and had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs and weapons possession".Belgal was arrested by police officers in New York in December 2023 and released "a few days later", according to the DHS.New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said there was also still a pending case against Belgal for criminal sale of a controlled substance in 2025. DHS has also alleged Belgal was associated with the Trinitarios, described by the US justice department as a transnational criminal group.Mullin said the DHS believed Belgal "has either indirect or direct knowledge" of a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer shooting, "and that's why he became a target".Mamdani is not the only New York official to have criticised the incident. Governor Kathy Hochul said federal officials needed to provide answers quickly about what happened. "New Yorkers have witnessed far too many acts of violence by a rogue federal agency and untrained agents that operate with impunity," Hochul said, adding that she had spoken to Mullin and Trump as well.There have been several high-profile shootings involving ICE officers this year, including one that caused the death of Renee Good in Minneapolis in January.

schema.headline: US immigration officials defend ICE agents who shot man while his child was in the car

title: Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire speaks to BBC from Ukrainian prison
description: A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was autho
body: A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was authorised by senior members of HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency.In an exclusive interview with the BBC from prison in Kyiv, facilitated by his lawyer, Vitalii Zhykovych has given his own account of the attempted assassination for the first time.Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries. Yermolayev later described their survival as "nothing short of a miracle".Zhykovych describes himself as a "freelancer" for Ukraine's SBU security service and says Anastasia Berezovska, the woman caught on camera planting the bomb in Monaco, was his "agent".A week after the bombing, Berezovska's body was discovered in the woods west of Kyiv with gunshot wounds to the head.But Zhykovych insists he did not send her to kill, and nor did he kill her.He was arrested and accused of her murder together with an active-duty intelligence officer from HUR called Vladyslav Reut.Reut initially confessed to investigators, and led them to the shallow grave. But days later in court, he changed his testimony to blame Zhykovych.The businessman himself, who renounced his Ukrainian passport some years ago and now has Cypriot citizenship, has dismissed multiple theories.They include the idea the attack might be linked to a struggle between organised crime groups involved in highly lucrative scam call-centres in Ukraine.Earlier this year, a court in Estonia convicted Yermolayev's son, Artur, of defrauding its citizens out of millions of euros through such "offisy", as the scam networks are known in Ukraine.Vadym Yermolayev told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper that he "never had anything to do with anything" in the case.Now Zhykovych has put forward his own theory to us.He alleges that Reut told him the bombing was in retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea", which he understood to mean Yermolayev was paying taxes to Russia from businesses in Russian-occupied Crimea."In my view, this constitutes grounds for the operation," he communicated from prison.The judge then interrupted, reminding him that he was addressing an open court.Zhykovych also revealed that Reut originally talked of two targets.When we asked, he said he could not disclose the second name. Other sources strongly suggest it was a pro-Russian blogger tried and convicted in absentia last year by Ukraine of treason.As the investigation continues – into both the bombing in Monaco and the murder in Ukraine - Berezovska's family have many questions of their own.The 39-year-old had been in Germany since early 2022, when she left Ukraine as a refugee with her young son.Zhykovych now claims she was living a double-life, working with him as an agent "against Muscovy" – meaning Russia.He said they had met online and told us the pair were working to "repel the armed aggression of the Russian Federation".Berezovska's husband has told the BBC that the allegation was "nonsense". He believes she was dragged, unwittingly, into the whole affair.Zhykovych says Berezovska called him the day after the Monaco attack, and when he asked why she had done it, she said Reut had promised her a huge fee. "$50,000 doesn't just lie on the streets," she supposedly explained.Residents in her village have told us that Berezovska was saving to buy a flat. But when she travelled to Ukraine to collect the money, she was lured into the woods and shot.Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko and Volodymyr Lozhko.

schema.headline: Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire speaks to BBC from Ukrainian prison

title: Powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake hits Panama, damaging buildings
description: Verified footage shows one side of a cathedral in Penonomé collapsed due to the shaking, as well as one of its spires.Another video showed a local hot
body: Verified footage shows one side of a cathedral in Penonomé collapsed due to the shaking, as well as one of its spires.Another video showed a local hotel had almost completely collapsed.Ricardo Brown, who lives in the southern Herrera province, told news agency Reuters that the earthquake had damaged several homes in his neighbourhood of Las Minas."We're scared. It's just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked and we're afraid it could fall on us," the 74-year-old said.The full extent of the damage it has caused is not yet clear, though several large aftershocks were also reported near the initial earthquake, potentially complicating the situation on the surface.The quake was registered as occurring at a depth of just 12km. The shallower the earthquake, the more likely it is to have more severe effects on the surface.Many people were evacuated from buildings in Panama City, about 200km from the epicentre, and were seen taking to the streets or sitting in nearby parks until the shaking had ceased.Damage in the capital appears to be limited to that caused by debris falling from roofs.Panama's President José Raúl Mulino said his entire government was mobilising in response to the earthquake, adding: "What happened should not be used to cause alarm or disorder."

schema.headline: Powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake hits Panama, damaging buildings

title: Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
description: Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the pa
body: Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

schema.headline: Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
